title: Application for a stay of execution of sentence of death

pages.text:
CAPITAL CASE
No. ______
______________________________________________________________________________ 
In the Supreme Court of the United States
______________________________________________________________________________ 
CHADWICK WILLACY,
Petitioner, 
v. 
SECRETARY, FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS,
Respondent. 
______________________________________________________________________________ 
ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE 
FLORIDA SUPREME COURT
______________________________________________________________________________ 
APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
______________________________________________________________________________ 
DEATH WARRANT SIGNED 
Execution Scheduled: April 21, 2026, at 6:00 PM ET
______________________________________________________________________________ 
To the Honorable Clarence Thomas, Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of 
the United States: 
The State of Florida has scheduled the execution of Petitioner Chadwick 
Willacy for Tuesday, April 21, 2026, at 6:00 PM ET. Pursuant to the Supreme Court 
Rule 23 and 28 U.S.C. § 2101(f), Mr. Willacy respectfully requests a stay of execution

2
pending the disposition of his Petition for a Writ of Certiorari accompanying this 
application.
STANDARDS FOR A STAY OF EXECUTION
The standards for granting a stay of execution are well established. Barefoot v. 
Estelle, 463 U.S. 880, 895 (1983). There “‘must be a reasonable probability that four 
members of the Court would consider the underlying issue sufficiently meritorious 
for the grant of certiorari or the notation of probable jurisdiction; there must be a 
significant possibility of reversal of the lower court’s decision; and there must be a 
likelihood that irreparable harm will result if that decision is not stayed.’” Id. (quoting 
White v. Florida, 458 U.S. 1301, 1302 (1982) (Powell, J., in chambers).
PETITIONER SHOULD BE GRANTED A STAY OF EXECUTION
The question raised in Mr. Willacy’s Petition for a Writ of Certiorari is 
sufficiently meritorious for a grant of a Writ of Certiorari. The underlying issue 
presents a significant, compelling question of constitutional law and a stay is 
necessary to avoid Mr. Willacy being executed in violation of the Eighth Amendment
to the United States Constitution before that question is resolved. Madison v. 
Alabama, 139 S. Ct. 718 (2019); Panetti v. Quarterman, 551 U.S. 930 (2007); Ford v. 
Wainwright, 477 U.S. 399 (1986).
It is indisputable that Mr. Willacy will be irreparably harmed if his execution 
is allowed to go forward. The balance of equities weighs heavily in favor of a stay. 
Florida’s interest in the timely enforcement of judgments handed down by its courts 
must be weighed against Mr. Willacy’s continued compelling interest in his life. See

3
Ohio Adult Parole Auth. v. Woodard, 523 U.S. 272, 289 (1998) (“[I]t is incorrect . . . to 
say that a prisoner has been deprived of all interest in his life before his execution.”) 
(O’Connor, J., plurality opinion). Florida has a minimal interest in finality and 
efficient enforcement of judgments, while Mr. Willacy has a right and significant 
interest in ensuring that his execution comports with the Constitution. In addition, 
the irreversible nature of the death penalty supports granting a stay. “[A] death 
sentence cannot begin to be carried out by the State while substantial legal issues 
remain outstanding.” Barefoot, 463 U.S. at 888. Mr. Willacy submits that there is a 
significant possibility of the lower court’s reversal, should this Court grant the 
request for a stay and review of the underlying petition. This Court’s intervention is 
urgently needed to prevent Mr. Willacy’s imminent execution despite the protections 
from the death penalty provided by the Eighth Amendment.
CONCLUSION
“The fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard
“at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.” Armstrong v. Manzo, 380 U.S. 
545, 552 (1965). Mr. Willacy’s meritorious issue cannot possibly be heard in a 
meaningful manner with just days left until his execution. The important 
constitutional issue presented by Mr. Willacy’s case requires a full appellate review 
that is not truncated by his imminent execution.
For the foregoing reasons, Mr. Willacy respectfully requests that this Court 
grant his application for a stay of execution scheduled for April 21, 2026, to address 
the compelling constitutional question in his case on the merits.

4
Respectfully submitted,
/s/ Melody J. Jacquay
MELODY JACQUAY-ACOSTA
